title: The Blue Hour of the old quarter
premise: Ivo Halloran, a bridge inspector who measures her own marriage in millimeters of metal fatigue, returns to the old quarter for her estranged father's funeral and finds a woman there who calls the family by a name Ivo has never heard. The stranger, Odile, was her father's second family in all but paperwork: a found household of strays he sheltered above his repair shop. As Ivo digs through photographs and ledgers, she learns her father secretly funded a neighborhood justice fund that settled grievances no court would touch, and that Odile now needs its last unspent sum to save the shop from a predatory developer. In forgiving the stranger in the old photographs, Ivo realizes the stranger is herself, the daughter her father wrote to every week and never sent them; the book ends with Ivo signing over her inheritance to keep both families' doors open, choosing belonging over the careful invisibility she built.
about_author: Kestrel Okonkwo is a former structural engineer who spent a decade inspecting bridges across coastal cities before turning to fiction full-time. Their stories examine how people load-bear for one another, and what quietly gives way.

chapters.title: Expansion Joints
chapters.summary: Ivo's POV. At her father's funeral in the old quarter, Ivo catalogues the mourners like defects on an inspection report, noting the distance between herself and her husband Marcus, who stayed home. A stranger, Odile, greets the family with an unfamiliar surname and knows details of Ivo's childhood no outsider should. Emotional beat: grief sharpened into suspicion as Ivo realizes her father kept a whole life she never measured.

chapters.title: The Ledger of Small Debts
chapters.summary: Ivo's POV, interleaved with her father's unsent letters. Sorting the shop's papers, Ivo discovers a ledger recording quiet settlements: rent paid, feuds mediated, a name crossed out beside her own. Odile explains the justice fund and asks for its remainder to fight the developer evicting the upstairs tenants. Emotional beat: resentment curdling into complicity as Ivo recognizes her father's handwriting in every mercy.

chapters.title: What the Photographs Kept
chapters.summary: Ivo's POV. Confronting Odile at the shop during the developer's inspection deadline, Ivo accuses her of fraud, until Odile produces a shoebox of photographs and the weekly letters addressed to 'Ivie,' the name nobody uses, stamped but never mailed. Marcus arrives unexpectedly, having read the letters Ivo left out. Emotional beat: the climax, where Ivo's armor of invisibility cracks and she must choose between grievance and inheritance.

chapters.title: Load-Bearing
chapters.summary: Ivo's POV, closing with one letter in her father's voice. Ivo signs the shop over to the tenants' trust, tells Marcus the truth about the distance between them, and stays through the blue hour to help repaint the storefront. She mails nothing back but writes a first letter of her own. Emotional beat: resolution, forgiveness, and the quiet weight of finally belonging somewhere by choice.
